arabic.note: Synthesised from per-sign recipes, not recorded.

msa.label: Modern Standard Arabic
msa.note: Maged (ar_SA) reading each letter's own Arabic name. For letter names the modern standard and the classical values coincide, so this is both the living pronunciation and the historical one — there is no second system to offer.

aramaic.note: Synthesised from per-sign recipes, not recorded.

modern.label: Modern Hebrew reading
modern.note: How these twenty-two glyphs are named today by the community that still writes them. This is Hebrew, not Aramaic surviving: the names are the Hebrew ones — Bet, Gimel, Dalet, Tsadi, Kuf, Tav against Beth, Gimel, Daleth, Sadhe, Qoph, Taw — and the phonology is Israeli, which has lost the pharyngeals, the emphatics and the uvular qoph. It earns the default click all the same, because Aramaic is read aloud in Jewish practice every day — the Kaddish, Kol Nidre, the Talmud, the Zohar — and it is read in exactly this voice. The strings are pointed so the voice cannot mistake a letter-name for the ordinary word it looks like.

imperial.label: Reconstructed Imperial Aramaic
imperial.note: The chancery Aramaic of the Achaemenid empire, and behind it the language of the bowls — with the pharyngeals, emphatics and uvular qoph that Modern Hebrew has lost, and with the letter names in their Aramaic rather than Hebrew shapes. Nothing Aramaic was ever recorded; every value here is reconstructed from Syriac spelling and from Hebrew and Arabic cognates. Arabic does most of the consonantal work because it is the only living language with the full set; Spanish, Italian and German are borrowed where Arabic's three vowels will not reach.

chinese.note: Synthesised from per-sign recipes, not recorded.

mandarin.label: Mandarin
mandarin.note: How the characters are read today in Beijing, and in the temples and academies of the mainland and Taiwan — the reading this hall's own pronunciation column already gives.

cantonese.label: Cantonese
cantonese.note: How the same characters are read in Hong Kong and Guangdong, where the Canon is also chanted — a living language, and on several points measurably closer to Middle Chinese than Mandarin is.

coptic.note: Synthesised from per-sign recipes, not recorded.

bohairic.label: Greco-Bohairic
bohairic.note: The pronunciation of the Coptic Orthodox liturgy as it is sung today. It is not ancient: it is the product of a nineteenth-century reform, begun by Iryan Moftah around 1858 under Patriarch Cyril IV, which re-read the Greek-derived letters with their MODERN Greek values in order to bring Coptic chant closer to the Greek church. It replaced an older reading, and it is the reason a Greek voice can pronounce most of this alphabet correctly.

old.label: Old Bohairic
old.note: How the letters were read before the nineteenth-century reform: reconstructed from philology, and supported by the traditional pronunciation that survived into the twentieth century in Upper Egyptian villages after Greco-Bohairic had taken the churches. Its organising fact is a series of aspirates — ⲫ ⲑ ⲭ ϭ against ⲡ ⲧ ⲕ ϫ — that the reform dissolved into fricatives and affricates. Vowel length is real here: ⲏ and ⲱ are long against ⲉ and ⲟ.

greek.note: Synthesised from per-letter recipes, not recorded.

modern.label: Modern Greek
modern.note: How a Greek speaker says the letter today — offered so the distance travelled can be heard.

ancient.label: Reconstructed Attic
ancient.note: Fifth-century Athens, following the reconstruction this hall’s alphabet already states. The ancient accent was melodic — a rise in pitch, not a beat of loudness — and these clips render it as stress. That is a trade rather than a hard limit: the one synthesis mode available that accepts a pitch contour speaks only American English sounds, so buying the accent would cost the trill, the geminates, the front rounded vowel and every unaspirated stop. And the reconstruction is itself an argument, not a recording.

hebrew.note: Synthesised from per-sign recipes, not recorded.

modern.label: Modern Israeli
modern.note: How the letters are named in Israel today, in the general standard register. Carmit is a Hebrew voice reading Hebrew, so this system is native rather than reconstructed — but every name is written with niqqud, because unpointed Hebrew is ambiguous and six of the letter names are spelled identically to ordinary words. This register has merged ḥet with khaf, qof with kaf and ṭet with tav, and has dropped ʿayin altogether; Mizrahi and Yemenite speech keeps those distinctions, and this voice does not.

tiberian.label: Reconstructed Tiberian
tiberian.note: The pronunciation of the Tiberian Masoretes, roughly tenth-century Galilee, following Geoffrey Khan's reconstruction. It keeps what Modern Israeli has lost: ʿayin as a voiced pharyngeal, ḥet as a pharyngeal fricative distinct from khaf, ṭet emphatic against a plain tav, qof uvular against kaf, and the full begadkefat alternation — so the letter names themselves end in [f], [θ], [ð] and [χ] where the modern names end in stops. Arabic carries every letter whose value turns on a pharyngeal, an emphatic, a uvular or a spirant; Spanish carries the letters where the vowel matters more; Hebrew carries the six letters where the two traditions genuinely agree. Arabic's three-vowel system cannot render Tiberian qamets [ɔː] or segol [ɛ], and that cost is stated on every letter where it is paid.

latin.note: Synthesised from per-sign recipes, not recorded.

ecclesiastical.label: Ecclesiastical
ecclesiastical.note: The Italianate Latin of the Roman rite and of virtually all choral singing: C and G soften before e and i, V is [v], AE is simply [e], H is silent, and vowel length is gone. Almost every clip here is an Italian voice reading an Italian spelling, because the two systems very nearly coincide. Understand 'ecclesiastical' as the modern Roman standard — medieval England, Germany and France each read Latin through their own vernacular, and the Italianate form became universal in the church only under Pius X.

classical.label: Reconstructed Classical
classical.note: Republican and Augustan Latin as reconstructed by Allen's Vox Latina and stated in this hall's own letter values: C always [k], G always [g], V as [w], AE as [ai], H a real breath, no palatalisation anywhere, p/t/k unaspirated, and vowel length phonemic. Italian supplies the unaspirated stops and the pure vowels, and its ch/gh and é/è spellings force the hard consonants and the close vowels; Spanish supplies the six consonant-final names, where its closed-syllable [ɛ] is Latin short e exactly; German supplies the one sound Italian cannot make, the [h]. Rate is the only handle on vowel length, so the long-vowel names are slowed.

sanskrit.note: Synthesised from per-sign recipes, not recorded.

traditional.label: Traditional recitation
traditional.note: The varṇamālā as a pandit recites it — the pronunciation the śikṣā treatises describe and Sanskrit recitation has carried unbroken. Lekha reads Devanagari, but reads it as Hindi, so four Hindi habits are worked around throughout. The name is given in its grammatical nominative (ककारः, not ककार) because Hindi deletes a word-final inherent a and the visarga blocks that deletion, restoring the final vowel Sanskrit requires — this is not a trick but what a grammarian actually says for 'the letter ka'. ऋ ॠ ऌ ॡ are handed to Czech and Slovak, the only installed languages with syllabic liquids, and Slovak alone with long ones. ऐ and औ are respelt आइ and आउ, their classical analysis as ā+i and ā+u, because Hindi has flattened them to [ɛː] and [ɔː]. And ष goes to a Russian voice, the only one that can make it audibly different from श. Two further signs are borrowed: ङ from Indonesian and ञ from Spanish, both for word-initial nasals Hindi cannot begin a word with. One caveat that applies to every Lekha clip here and cannot be tested by ear from this machine: if the voice drops the final visarga instead of sounding it, these fall back to the plain Hindi reading and the restored inherent vowel is lost.

modern.label: Modern North Indian
modern.note: The same fifty signs read as a Hindi speaker reads them, which is how most of India pronounces the Sanskrit alphabet today. Nothing here is engineered: Lekha reading plain Devanagari simply IS this pronunciation. The final inherent a falls away, ऋ is [rɪ], ऐ and औ are the monophthongs [ɛː] and [ɔː], ष is merged into श, and फ is given its nuqta because modern speech makes it [f]. On some thirty consonants the two systems agree entirely and differ only in that dropped final vowel — that agreement is itself worth hearing, since it is what has been kept. The divergences are the short list the hall's own entries name: ri for ṛ, the flattened diphthongs, f for ph, the lost sibilant, and the letters ङ ञ ऌ ॡ ळ that Hindi has no living use for at all.

slavonic.note: Synthesised from per-sign recipes, not recorded.

recension.label: Church Slavonic today
recension.note: The Russian recension — how the letters are named and read in the Slavonic sung in Moscow and Kyiv now. This is one living reading, not the only one: the Serbian and Bulgarian recensions differ, and no voice for either is installed on this machine. Milena reads Cyrillic as RUSSIAN, which is right for the consonants and wrong for the vowels: the recension's own rule is оканье, unstressed о read as [o] and never as [a], and that rule cannot be imposed on her — seven names say so.

ocs.label: Old Church Slavonic, reconstructed
ocs.note: The tenth-century canon as Slavists read it aloud: nasal vowels sounding, [dz] and [ʃt] intact, jers still vowels. Russian is almost useless here — it deletes nine of these letters and reduces every unstressed vowel — so the reconstruction is built on Polish, the only living language with the nasals, [ɨ], [dz] and [dʑ] and no vowel reduction, and on Czech, which supplies the postalveolar sibilants, phonemic vowel length and syllabic [r̩] that Polish lacks. Two letters are voiced elsewhere, each for a stated reason.
